                             INTRODUCTION AND ISSUES ROADMAP

        Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro (“EMM” or the “Company”) respectfully

submits this Initial Post-Hearing Brief (“Brief”) to the Missouri Public Service Commission

(“Commission”). 1

        This rate case is about the affordable, reliable, and sustainable service the Company’s

customers expect and deserve. In 2025, the Company had the 16th lowest average residential bill

among the 100 largest investor-owned electric utilities with bundled sales. 2 On February 6, 2026,

the Company filed its first general rate case in four years, as required by the statute governing its

fuel adjustment clause (“FAC”). 3 In the four years since its last rate case, the Company has focused

on affordability, reliability, and sustainability for all customers in its service territory. It continues

to deliver that service through the investments in this case.

        “Evergy Missouri Metro’s total rates decreased by 2.2% over the period 2017 through

October 2025, while the rates of electric utilities in peer states have increased by an average of

18.8%,” during a period in which inflation increased by approximately 29%. 4 Figure 1, from the

direct testimony of Kevin Gunn (Vice President, Regulatory and Government Affairs), shows that

comparison state by state.

The Company filed this case originally requesting a revenue requirement increase of $140.4

Subsection B shows how the Company’s $88.9 million figure is comprised. If approved, the $88.9

million increase in the revenue requirement would result in a cumulative 9.6% change since the

end of 2017, equal to a 2.3% annual increase since the 2022 rate case and a 1.0% annual increase

since 2017. 9 This is well below regional peer utilities and far below inflation over the same periods.

        If granted, the requested increase recovers the cost of new infrastructure investments that

enhance reliability and customer service. These new infrastructure investments are needed to

C.      Summary of Contested Issues for Commission Resolution

Each numbered section below provides a high-level summary of the remaining contested issues in

        1.       Large Load Power Service Issues (Section I)(pp. 24-61)

        The Company respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the LLPS Stipulation. It

passes the benefit of large load growth to the Company’s other customers in three primary ways,

among others. It credits $60 million of large load revenue against what those customers pay, keeps

large load customers in the FAC on terms that favor other customers, and shares large load earnings

with customers. This is a transitional case. Less than a year ago, the Commission approved

Schedule LLPS as a package. 52 Through the Non-Unanimous Global Stipulation and Agreement

(the “Global Stipulation”) in Case No. EO-2025-0154, it reserved any modifications of LLPS cost

allocation, rate design, and class cost of service for the first rate case in which a Schedule LLPS

customer of 75 megawatts (“MW”) or more is reflected in the test year. 53 No LLPS customer is

in EMM’s test year—the twelve months ending June 30, 2025—because the Schedule LLPS tariff

        The $60 million credit is the revenue of the Company’s first LLPS customer (“Customer

A”) at the June 30, 2026, true-up, based on its known and measurable billing determinants (Issue

3.A). Because none of the Company’s revenue requirement is caused by LLPS load, every dollar

Staff’s competing figure is not known and measurable, because it multiplies a contract capacity

only tariff change settles on a single reading of the minimum bill, which raises LLPS bills during

the ramp.

        The Company serves Schedule LLPS customers from the same system as every other

customer. It sells its generation into the SPP market and buys the energy for all of its load from

that market, so sales and purchases largely net out. What remains is the fuel cost of running the

Company’s own generators, which serve every customer. LLPS customers should therefore

remain in EMM’s FAC, as Schedule LLPS was designed (Issue 25). The LLPS Stipulation’s FAC

terms favor other customers in two ways. First, fuel cost swings related to the LLPS allocated

portion are shared 90/10% rather than 95/5%. The Company therefore absorbs more of any

increase and the single fuel adjustment rate every customer pays is lower. Second, the base factor

is built from Staff’s own fuel costs and leaves LLPS customers’ fuel out of it, so nothing is

recovered twice. Staff’s own witness agreed that the energy rate LLPS customers pay and the cost

of the energy to serve them come out about even.

          Finally, the LLPS Stipulation shares large load earnings with customers through the

Earnings Review Surveillance mechanism (“ERS”) (Issue 37.A). An authorized return is an

opportunity to earn, and large load growth gives the Company a realistic chance to earn it. The

ERS keeps that opportunity in place and provides a customer sharing mechanism as well. Sharing

occurs when the Company’s earned ROE exceeds the ROE authorized in this case by more than

20 basis points and LLPS base rate revenue exceeds the $60 million in rates. Customers then

receive 65% of the earnings above that threshold through a future rate case, with any share above

50% directed to low-income customers. That way, sharing tracks large load growth rather than

weather or expense variation. The Commission approved a mechanism of substantially the same

design for Ameren Missouri last year, and the Large Load Order contemplated an earnings-sharing

mechanism in a future rate case after LLPS customers begin receiving service. 55

         2.     Non-LLPS FAC Issues (Section II)(pp. 61-68)

non-LLPS customers, including the 95%/5% sharing mechanism, and no party objected to those

terms.

        3.       Cost of Capital (Section III)(pp. 68-86)

        The Company respectfully requests that the Commission authorize a 10.50% ROE on the

Company’s actual capital structure of 52.19% equity (Issues 1.A and 1.C). Staff and OPC

recommend 9.73% and 9.25%, respectively, on analyses that have not changed since December.

However, between December 31, 2025, and the June 30, 2026, true-up the 30-year Treasury yield

rose 7 basis points and the 10-year Treasury yield rose 26 basis points. Since the true-up, interest

rates and the costs of raising capital have continued to rise. Between June 30 and October 30, 2026,

the 30-year Treasury yield rose 40 basis points and the 10-year Treasury yield rose 50 basis

points. 57

        The capital structure should be the Company’s actual per-book structure at true-up: 52.19%

common equity and 47.81% long-term debt. Staff recommends the same. OPC would instead

impute an adjusted version of Evergy, Inc.’s consolidated structure, 45% equity and 55% debt.

The Company issues its own debt, carries no parent guarantee, and holds stand-alone credit ratings

stronger than its parent’s. The cost of debt, 4.54%, is not in dispute.

       Staff witness Dr. Seoung Joun Won recommends 9.73%, but he rests that figure on a single

bond yield risk premium analysis. His mean discounted cash flow result was 8.18% and the

average of his mean DCF and capital asset pricing model results was 8.67%. These results are

below any ROE authorized for a vertically integrated electric utility since 1980. OPC witness

David Murray recommends 9.25%, a figure none of his own studies supports. Dr. Won’s analysis

should be given limited weight given his narrow analysis. However, as considered, his midpoint

should be updated to reflect changes in market conditions since December 2025, and Mr. Murray’s

unsupported recommendation should be disregarded.

       4.      Income Taxes (Section IV)(pp. 86-91)

       The Company respectfully requests that the Commission reject OPC’s two income tax

adjustments, which Staff also opposes (Issues 15.A.i and 15.C). Staff’s reconciliation values them

at $5,437,280 and $2,941,318 of revenue requirement. The Partial Stipulation resolves the other

income tax sub-issues between the Company and Staff, and OPC does not oppose it. First, OPC

would reduce income tax expense by a levelized amount of the tax losses recorded when an asset

retires early. However, customers have already received the tax benefit on the losses through

accumulated deferred income taxes, which reduce rate base. OPC’s adjustment to include the tax

 benefits again as an offset to income tax expense would inappropriately include the tax benefits on

losses twice.

           Second, OPC would remove from rate base the deficient deferred income taxes created by

the federal and Missouri income tax rate reductions on the Company’s net operating losses.

However, the Commission has already set the treatment of that balance. The Company’s 2018 rate

case set the amortization of the federal amount, and the stipulation the Commission approved in

the 2022 rate case set a four-year amortization of the Missouri amount. As Staff testified, OPC

does not explain why that treatment should change now.

           5.      Fuel and Purchased Power (Section V)(pp. 91-92)

           The Commission should adopt Staff’s fuel and purchased power costs, which the LLPS

Stipulation adopts and no other party contests (Issue 5). That includes Staff’s total variable fuel

and purchased power cost, as agreed in the LLPS Stipulation, with the Missouri jurisdictional

amount as Staff’s reconciliation states. It also includes Staff’s fuel prices, normalized market

prices, and historical transmission congestion rights amount.

           6.      MEEIA Margin Rates (Section VI)(pp. 93-96)

           The Commission should approve the Company’s method for calculating the net margin

rates used in its Demand Side Investment Mechanism Rider under the Missouri Energy Efficiency

Investment Act (“MEEIA”) (Issue 42). 58 Staff does not oppose the Company’s method, and the

Commission should approve it. Staff also states that the net margin rates should be recalculated

on the final rates in this case, which the Company’s tariff already requires.

         7.       PISA (Section VII)(pp. 96-97)

        The Company respectfully requests that the Commission include in rate base the PISA

deferral balance in Exhibit B to the Partial Stipulation (Issue 18.B). Section 393.1400 59 requires

that balance be included in rate base without offset or adjustment, except for a prudence

disallowance the Commission has ordered. OPC’s only objection is to remove the distribution and

transmission projects it asks the Commission to disallow. Those disallowances should be rejected

for the reasons summarized in Subsection C.8, below. In short, OPC identifies no decision that

was unreasonable when it was made, and its own analysis shows reliability improved on the laterals

it would disallow. Its value-exceeds-cost test did not exist when the investments were made, and

the Commission has never adopted it. If the Commission were to order a disallowance (which the

Company’s evidence demonstrates it should not), Partial Stipulation ¶ 7 provides for an adjustment

removing the related PISA deferral, computed for the specific projects from their in-service dates

and depreciation rates.

        8.       Rate Base and Asset Management (Section VIII)(pp. 97-119)

        The Company respectfully requests that the Commission: (1) include the CWIP for Mullin

Creek No. 2 in rate base, (2) reject Staff’s retired plant adjustment, and (3) reject OPC’s

transmission and distribution disallowances. The investments at issue here keep the Company’s

service reliable, from a new generating unit to the replacement of aging poles, lines, and

transformers.

in setting the appropriate return on common equity is that the return be reasonably sufficient to
